list.listitem: Because of the low incidence of this locally aggressive but benign proliferative disease of the synovium, a high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis of pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS). C
MRI is the imaging study of choice when PVNS is suspected after history, physical examination, and plain radiographs. B
Synovial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of PVNS. B

Most patients will require surgical treatment, which may include synovectomy (open versus arthroscopic, partial versus total) with or without postoperative adjuvant therapy (intra-articular versus external beam radiation). C
High recurrence rates are associated with all treatments of diffuse PVNS, B warranting close surveillance for recurrent symptoms or MRI findings. C

background.definition: PVNS is a rare, benign, but locally aggressive synovial proliferative disorder that can occur in all joints, tendon sheaths, and bursae, with a predilection for the knee.

list.listitem: The diffuse villous form of PVNS accounts for the majority of cases.
The overall annual incidence of PVNS is 2 cases per 1 million population.
Age of onset is typically between 20 and 40 years.
The etiology of PVNS is uncertain. The knee joint is most often affected (approximately 80%), followed by the hip and finger synovial structures; involvement of the shoulder, foot, and ankle is rare.
PVNS was originally thought to be an inflammatory reaction to an unknown cause.
More recent evidence of monoclonal origin and centrifugal growth patterns with capacity to erode surrounding tissues suggests a neoplastic process.
PVNS is characterized by hypervascular proliferative synovium containing multinucleated giant cells, macrophages, and hemosiderin. The multinucleated cells express features of osteoclasts.
The abundant presence of hemosiderin in the macrophages and surrounding tissues gives the characteristic brown pigmented appearance.

PVNS occurs in 2 forms: the diffuse villous form typically involves large joints, while the localized nodular form typically occurs around the small joints of the hands and feet. Both forms usually involve a single joint.
PVNS typically invades local tissues, including subchondral bone with resultant cyst formation.
Chronic or recurrent monoarticular joint pain, swelling, and stiffness, especially of the knee, should prompt consideration of PVNS. C
Plain radiographs showing soft tissue swelling, periarticular bone erosions, or subchondral cysts should prompt MRI evaluation for PVNS. C

MRI findings of low signal intensity on T1-weighted and T2-weighted images, hyperplastic synovium, and bony erosions are highly suspicious for PVNS. MRI is the imaging method of choice when radiographs are suggestive of PVNS. B
The diagnosis is often delayed; average delay is 3 years.

Differential.Differential_Features: Age more than 50 years; radiographic joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis
Associated with uveitis, digestive symptoms, rashes, HLA-B27
Local inflammatory signs; synovial cultures positive
Multiple calcified or osseous loose bodies on plain radiographs
Characteristic appearance and location of bony lesions on radiographs
Radiographic or MRI findings of subchondral bone collapse
Most common in adolescents; commonly metastasizes to lymph nodes

list.listitem: Most cases are unilateral, monoarticular, and confined to large joints, with 80% of cases occurring in the knee. Because of the low incidence and clinical heterogeneity of PVNS, a high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis.
Less commonly involved joints include (in order of frequency) the hip, ankle, and the shoulder.
The localized form of PVNS of the knee often presents with mechanical symptoms from a mass effect, and may mimic meniscal tears or loose bodies.
Diffuse PVNS is more common, and presents with insidious onset of knee swelling, diffuse pain, and stiffness without history of trauma.
Physical examination often reveals a knee effusion with diffused tenderness and loss of motion.
Joint pain and effusion with hemarthrosis are the most common presenting signs.
A palpable mass may occasionally be present.
Plain radiographs are nonspecific for PVNS, but may show periarticular soft tissue density in up to 80% of cases.
MRI is the imaging modality of choice, and is diagnostic in more than 95% of cases.
CT is valuable in delineating bone cysts and erosions, and is useful for needle biopsy guidance and preoperative planning.
Arthrocentesis yields blood-tinged synovial fluid in 44% to 69% of cases.
Synovial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of PVNS, showing proliferative sheets of mononuclear cells within the synovium.
See the algorithm in for a suggested approach to diagnosis, and see the algorithm in for a suggested approach to treatment.
Synovial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis.
Nonoperative treatments such as antiinflammatory medications, activity modification, and steroid injections have limited benefit in PVNS. C
Selection of the appropriate treatment for PVNS requires localization and classification of the lesion and knowledge of the patient's prior clinical course. C

Most patients will require surgical treatment that must be tailored to the disease presentation; options include open or arthroscopic total or partial synovectomy, with or without adjuvant therapies. C
Anti-inflammatory medications and corticosteroid injections have limited benefit.
Most patients will require surgical treatment that must be tailored to the disease presentation.
Surgical treatment options include open or arthroscopic total or partial synovectomy.
High recurrence rates are associated with all treatments of diffuse PVNS, and suspected cases of recurrence warrant re-evaluation by MRI.
See the algorithm in for a suggested approach to treatment of PVNS of the knee.
Total knee arthoplasty may be an option for PVNS of the knee.
Activity modification and physical therapy are of limited benefit.
Intra-articular radioisotope injection and external beam radiation may be beneficial adjuvant therapy for extensive diffuse and recurrent PVNS of the knee.

A meta-analysis of 35 observational studies which included 630 patients showed that 137 (21.8%) had a recurrence after synovectomy alone. For patients with the diffuse form of PVNS, low-quality evidence suggested that the rate of recurrence was reduced by both open synovectomy (odds ratio = 0.47; 95% CI 0.25-0.90; p = 0.024) and combined open and arthroscopic synovectomy (odds ratio = 0.19; 95% CI 0.06-0.58; p = 0.003) compared with arthroscopic surgery alone. Very low-quality evidence suggested that the rate of recurrence of DPVNS was reduced by peri-operative radiotherapy (odds ratio = 0.31; 95% CI 0.14-0.70; p = 0.01). Very low-quality evidence suggested that the rate of recurrence of localized PVNS was not related to the surgical approach.

While radiosynoviorthesis and external beam radiation have been used for recalcitrant disease, recent understanding of the colony stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) pathway and its paracrine and autocrine roles in PVNS has led to the development of targeted inhibitors which may play an increasing role for these targeted agents, especially in diffuse and/or refractory disease. Their optimal role and efficacy remain unclear due to limited numbers of high-quality studies and contradictory results.
Refer patient to orthopedic surgeon if PVNS is suspected after history, physical examination, and MRI findings.
High recurrence rates (up to 45%) are associated with all treatments of diffuse PVNS and may require repeat synovectomy and adjuvant therapy. B
Recurrent postoperative knee pain or effusions warrant re-evaluation by MRI. C
When synovectomy fails to relieve all symptoms in patients with significant destructive changes in the joint, arthrodesis or total joint replacement should be considered. B

cell.label: Suspected pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS): chronic/recurrent monoarticular joint pain, swelling, and stiffness (especially in the knee); mechanical symptoms of mass effect; joint effusion with diffuse tenderness and loss of motion.
Plain radiographs typical of PVNS? (Soft tissue swelling, periarticular bone erosions, subchondral cysts.)
MRI results typical of PVNS? (Effusion, low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, hyperplastic synovium, bony erosions.)
Synovial biopsy typical for PVNS? (Proliferative sheets of mononuclear cells within the synovium, presence of hemosiderin.)
Synovectomy: Open versus arthroscopic, with or without adjuvant therapy.
Type of PVNS of the knee.
Repeat total synovectomy; consider adjuvant therapy.
